newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: YEAREND - Misfits with grudges were year's worst killers.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Misfits with grudges were year's worst killers.

text.p: In 1996, small-town misfits exacted payment in blood for their grievances.

On a clear March morning, 43-year-old Thomas Hamilton strode into a primary school in the Scottish town of Dunblane. In just four minutes he shot dead 16 children and their teacher before turning a gun on himself.

Six weeks later on the other side of the world, Martin Bryant walked into a cafe on the tranquil island state of Tasmania and began pumping bullets into tourists having lunch by the ruins of an old penal colony.
Within two minutes 20 people were dead. By the time of his arrest the next day, the laughing gunman of Port Arthur had killed 35 people to become Australia's worst mass murderer.

Hamilton and Bryant both fitted the mould of the dangerous misfit, loners with a grudge against society and the weapons to avenge it. Both forced their countries to review their laws on gun ownership.
But although their actions shocked the world, they were not alone in plumbing the depths of darkness. And all too often in 1996 children bore the brunt of adult anger and perversion.
With crime figures in the United States falling -- America for once seemed strangely short of gruesome killings -- some of the year's sickest crimes occurred in the most unlikely places.
PAEDOPHILIA

Better known for beer and bureaucrats than for death and depravity, Belgium hit the headlines in August when two sexually-abused girls were rescued from a makeshift dungeon and police unearthed the corpses of four others.

The Dutroux affair, named after chief suspect Marc Dutroux, a convicted rapist, sparked an international hunt for links to paedophile rings in other countries and shook Belgium to its normally placid core.
As delegates met in Stockholm for the first world conference on the sexual exploitation of children, the breaking Belgian scandal showed that paedophilia was not just a remote Third World issue.
SERIAL KILLINGS
Liberated from their historical shackles, Russia and South Africa fought to retain international confidence against a background of violence and rising crime.
Police last month found what they believe to be the 14th victim of a Johannesburg serial killer, while another South African pleaded not guilty to 38 murders and 40 rapes.
Faced with the crime wave some South African residents even began to plant landmines in their gardens to protect themselves against intruders.

In Costa Rica police said that a serial killer known as "The Psychopath" may have claimed more than 30 victims. The killer preys on young women and their lovers while they are kissing in secluded places.

In North Carolina, the trial began of Henry Wallace, a former fast food worker accused of using brassieres and bath towels to strangle nine women during an alleged two-year murder spree between 1992 and 1994.
TASMANIAN ANGUISH
Most devastating, though, were the killings at the Port Arthur convict prison, which for some sounded the death knell of Australia's age of innocence.

Bryant, an unemployed 29-year-old with no close family ties, had travelled the world looking for people to talk to after having a fortune left to him by an older female companion. According to a medical report read out in court, he became "enraged by the frequency with which people would turn away".
On April 28 in the Broad Arrow Cafe, he vented his frustrations by slaughtering 20 people with a powerful semi-automatic rifle.

Twelve of his victims were finished off in just 15 seconds, some still holding their knife and fork. Others were hunted like animals in the nearby bush, including a six-year-old girl killed as she hid behind a tree.
After his crime, Bryant did little to calm Tasmania's anguish, initially pleading not guilty to 35 counts of murder and 20 of attempted murder.
He changed his plea last month, laughing in court as the individual counts were read to him.

The killings produced a strong backlash against lax gun ownership laws and, despite rural opposition, Prime Minister John Howard pushed through a ban on almost all self-loading guns combined with a costly buyback of banned weapons.
MASSACRE OF THE INNOCENTS
After the suicide of serial killer Fred West and the jailing of his wife Rosemary in 1995, the people of Britain probably felt they had had their fill of horrors.
Then came Dunblane's "slaughter of the innocents".
Hamilton had four handguns and more than 700 rounds of ammunition when he murdered 16 five and six-year-olds as they played in a school gym.
All of his weapons were legally owned, even though witnesses said Hamilton was known to harbour a sick fascination for small boys and a deep grudge from having been sacked as a scoutmaster.
Days before the killings, Hamilton had even written to Britain's Queen Elizabeth insisting he was no "pervert".

The Dunblane outcry forced the British government to look again at its gun laws, already among Europe's tightest and in November parliament voted to ban all handguns except for the smallest .22 calibre pistols.
HOUSE OF HORRORS
Yet if Dunblane was Britain's worst mass murder, the "House of Horrors" of Fred and Rosemary West, in the western English town of Gloucester, remained the most macabre crime scene in modern memory.

In October, Britain tried literally to obliterate all trace of it when the building was demolished and bricks and masonry from the house of so many murders were ground to dust to deter souvenir hunters.
In November, the gruesome saga was reopened when John West was found hanging just three miles (five km) from his brother Fred's home.
West was awaiting verdict on charges he had raped his niece at the Gloucester house where Fred and Rosemary had raped, tortured and murdered women over the years.
Detective Superintendent John Bennett said the apparent suicide was "another tragedy in what seems to be an endless sequence of sad events".
The sad events went on and on, with children time and again falling victim to grown-up lusts. Paedophile rings were uncovered not just in Belgium but in Poland, France, Austria and elsewhere.
In May, two paedophiles who abducted, raped and killed an impish-looking British nine-year-old were jailed for life.
The pair had cruised the streets looking at young boys when they spotted Daniel Handley and decided he was the perfect subject for their fantasy of abducting a blue-eyed boy for assault and murder.

Daniel was buggered repeatedly while the pair videoed each other in action. Moments before his death he had asked: "Are you going to kill me?". His tormentors had assured Daniel death was not in store.
